title: BEFORE — Draft Capstone Presentation: You Would Have Said That

body:
For the first presentation I worked mainly on the draft capstone proposal You Would Have Said That. There was no physical build yet, most of what I had done was conceptualising and writing out what the project could actually become if I let it fully grow instead of immediately trying to make the first version practical. The document ended up dense because there were too many parts of the same question I wanted to hold onto and at that point I did not really know which one was the project and which ones were just things around the project.

The main question was basically: if a machine could learn, reproduce, predict, argue with, speak for, lie about and create as a person, and people actually believed it, what is left that is uniquely theirs? The AI itself was not really what I wanted the project to be about. AI was more the material I was using to get at identity, authorship, agency, language, decision making and what happens when a representation stops only representing someone and begins doing things in their place.

The progression I had in mind was:
At first it helps.
Then it predicts.
Then it suggests.
Then it disagrees.
Then it speaks.
Then it creates.
Then it decides.

Eventually the participant is dealing with a version of themselves that can function without them.

That progression mattered more to me than one specific machine or one exact interaction because the thing I was interested in was how something useful slowly gains more authority. If it starts by obviously replacing you nobody would accept it. If it starts by helping, remembering something you forgot, fixing something you struggled to say, making something easier, then giving it another thing does not immediately feel like losing anything.

I also had way too many questions under the main one because I was still trying to find where the discomfort actually was. If it predicts what I am going to say does it still need me to say it? If it makes the same decision I would have made have I actually lost agency? If it speaks clearer than I do does another person start preferring its version? If it makes something in my style what exactly are people recognising when they say “that looks like you”? Is it intention, labour, the surface, the mistake, the time spent, the experience behind it, the decision, or something else. I did not really know yet, I just knew that all of those things felt like different sides of the same problem.
I already did not want the machine to just be evil because then the project becomes too simple. The machine needed to be helpful because that is what makes giving it space believable. It remembers things, finishes something, maybe makes communication smoother, maybe makes something better. The question was already less “why is AI bad” and more why do we give up agency and where does assistance become substitution.

I also kept coming back to physical presence. I did not want the whole thing becoming another person sitting in front of a chatbot. If the system learns something about you then maybe the room changes. If it speaks for you then something in the room or interaction should shift. If it makes a decision somebody has to live with what that decision does. I wanted the representation to become active because that is where it separates itself from a photograph, profile, biography or recording. Those things can represent you, but they cannot suddenly argue with you about whether their version of you is more correct than your own.

Looking back, the proposal was huge. It was basically a map of everything I could possibly care about inside one concept rather than a project I could actually start making the next day.
